date_note: SOCRadar's post of 26 November; the campaign it describes ran August to September 2026.
title: SOCRadar: RedOps campaign hit Thai and Philippine government and military-affiliated networks
summary: SOCRadar says its RedOps campaign, active August to September 2026, had five confirmed intrusions in Thailand and the Philippines, including a military-affiliated organisation and a legislative organisation in Thailand. SOCRadar links it to WeaveLotus with moderate confidence and to OceanLotus (APT32) with low confidence, and says this does not conclusively establish state sponsorship.
plain: SOCRadar says a campaign it calls RedOps made five confirmed intrusions into Thai and Philippine government-linked networks in August and September 2026. It links the campaign to WeaveLotus with moderate confidence.
exec: SOCRadar reports five confirmed intrusions at government and military-affiliated bodies in Thailand and the Philippines.
action: SOCRadar advises patching internet-facing open-source applications, prioritising GeoServer and osTicket, and removing default credentials such as those on JasperReports.

validation.note: SOCRadar (the investigating firm, primary source) and Cyber Security News both report the campaign; Cyber Security News relays SOCRadar's research.

review.note: figure: key_findings counts set to the source's exact 31,418 files and 349,782 records; title, date, five intrusions, confidence levels, caveat and action checked against SOCRadar and Cyber Security News

key_findings: SOCRadar attributes the RedOps campaign, active August to September 2026, with moderate confidence to WeaveLotus, targeting government, military and legislative bodies.
SOCRadar reports five confirmed intrusions in Thailand and the Philippines, and reconnaissance of more than 30 Indonesian government organisations with no intrusion following.

SOCRadar says it saw collection of about 19 GB of documents from a Thai legislative organisation, 31,418 files from a Thai military organisation and 349,782 records from a Thai government application.
Entry was through exposed open-source web applications: GeoServer, JasperReports with default credentials, osTicket and a Laravel app with debug mode on.
Intrusions were chained: access in one environment led to a third-party document system and administrator credentials for another agency.
recommendations: Patch internet-facing open-source applications, starting with GeoServer and osTicket.
Remove default credentials, such as those on JasperReports.
Disable debug mode on production Laravel applications.
Monitor for unusual authentication activity, password spraying and ROPC token requests.
Block or alert on outbound SSH over port 443, SOCKS proxies and bulk data transfers.
